title: Peripheral neuropathy in severe COVID‐19 resolved with therapeutic plasma exchange
case_prompt:
A 44-year-old previously healthy man presented in June 2020 with 12 days of fever (peak 38.3°C), persistent cough, anosmia, diarrhea, myalgias, and progressive bilateral lower-limb weakness. He had unprotected contact with his SARS-CoV-2–positive brother one week before symptom onset.

On examination, temperature was 38.1°C, other vital signs were within normal limits, and oxygen saturation was 78% on room air; high-flow nasal cannula (60 L/min, FiO2 40%) improved SpO2 to 89%. Neurologic examination revealed bilateral lower-limb muscle strength of 3/5, gait ataxia, and areflexia at the knees and ankles; sensation was intact. Lung auscultation showed bilateral crackles at the bases.

Emergency electromyography of the lower limbs demonstrated delayed distal latencies with normal conduction velocities. Upper limbs were not tested; no biopsy was performed. Laboratory studies showed lymphocytopenia (0.51 × 10^9/L), elevated C-reactive protein (247 mg/L), lactate dehydrogenase (1222 U/L), D-dimer (3.6 μg/mL), ferritin (1123 ng/mL), interleukin-6 (778 pg/mL), and slight creatine kinase elevation (616 U/L); renal and hepatic function were otherwise normal. ADAMTS13 activity was reduced at 8% with normal antibody levels. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed normal cell count and protein. SARS-CoV-2 infection was confirmed by RT-PCR. Chest CT showed bilateral peripheral ground-glass opacities without pulmonary embolism. Fourteen hours after presentation, he developed severe hypoxia (SpO2/FiO2 100) and septic shock, necessitating intubation and ICU transfer, where he received ARDS-net ventilation, prone positioning, antiviral agents, broad-spectrum antibiotics, vasopressors, hydrocortisone, and prophylactic anticoagulation.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Consideration of demyelinating versus axonal peripheral neuropathy — “our differential diagnosis included peripheral neuropathy (demyelinating versus axonal) accordingly.”  
2. Exclusion of central nervous system pathology — “He had no sensory deficits and no other central nervous system or other neurological signs and symptoms” and “CSF analysis revealed a normal cell count … and protein.”  
3. Consideration of Guillain–Barré syndrome variant despite atypical features — “We cannot exclude Guillain–Barré syndrome… although our patient did not have typical manifestations, the possibility of a GBS variant cannot be omitted.”
